page.title: Trajectory Postprocessing
page.description: Independent research into smooth, impact-preserving trajectory reconstruction using synthetic motion and existing detection data.
page.role: Independent research: synthetic training data, noise modeling, sequence-model design, loss design, and integration into the keypoint postprocessing workflow.

sections.title: Abstract
paragraphs: Frame-by-frame detection produced jittery golf swing trajectories under blur, occlusion, and unstable lighting, limiting reliable motion analysis. I independently developed a sequence model using synthetic 3D swings and realistic detection noise, requiring no new data collection or annotation. The model resolved approximately 80% of the jittery cases evaluated while preserving sharp motion around impact, and became part of the product’s keypoint processing workflow.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Single-frame detections can vary with small pixel changes, lighting flicker, extreme motion blur, occlusion, and a club leaving the image. These errors accumulate into jittery trajectories. Dropped video frames introduce additional gaps, while low frame rates leave sparse observations of rapid movement.

The Kalman-based approaches we evaluated required settings that varied with frame rate and swing phase. Abrupt changes in speed, direction, and acceleration challenged their motion assumptions. In down-the-line views, sparse sampling around impact can produce a sharp turn that excessive smoothing distorts.
My research question was: Can a sequence model trained on synthetic motion recover smooth, plausible trajectories from noisy detections while retaining the sharp changes that matter at impact?

sections.title: Methods

subsections.title: Replace unavailable reference sequences with synthetic motion
paragraphs: Manual annotation could not supply complete trajectories with sufficiently consistent motion across frames. I used observations of golf swings to build a generator of varied 3D club paths. Projecting those paths through virtual cameras provided clean 2D training targets without collecting or labeling new footage.

subsections.title: Connect synthetic training to observed errors
paragraphs: A clean trajectory alone does not represent detector failures. I extracted error patterns by comparing existing model predictions with existing manual annotations, then combined those observations with additional noise patterns I designed. Each corrupted input retained its corresponding clean target.

subsections.title: Learn reconstruction at the sequence level
paragraphs: I designed the model and loss function to reconstruct motion from the noisy sequence. Task-specific regularization complemented the regression objective and guided convergence toward plausible trajectories. The design goal was to reduce jitter and reject outliers while retaining the sensitive geometry around impact.

subsections.title: Assess the reconstructed trajectory
paragraphs: I examined before-and-after trajectories across frame rates, camera views, blur, occlusion, and frame-boundary failures. The final criterion was trajectory smoothness together with preservation of impact motion. I also evaluated the model on body-joint sequences to assess whether the approach extended beyond the club.

sections.note: Architecture, loss formulations, and proprietary training details are omitted. The focus here is the reasoning behind the data and reconstruction approach.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: The model produced smoother trajectories, rejected outliers, and retained sharp motion near impact across the footage evaluated. It also stabilized body-joint sequences and entered the standard keypoint workflow.

subsections.title: What the results suggest
paragraphs: The observed results support using synthetic clean motion and realistic corruption to train sequence-level reconstruction when reliable reference trajectories are unavailable. Compared with the conventional filters we tried, the model covered a broader range of recording conditions without the same repeated parameter tuning.

subsections.title: Limitations
paragraphs: Synthetic motion and camera sampling cannot fully represent real swings. Noise extracted from a particular detector may also limit transfer to different error distributions. Positions reconstructed through occlusion or outside the frame remain estimates; greater smoothness alone does not establish positional accuracy.

subsections.title: CI/CD and MLOps implications
paragraphs: The model became a reusable postprocessing stage for club and body keypoints. The synthetic-data generator, noise pipeline, and reconstruction model provide repeatable components for MLOps iteration. Future CI/CD integration could use fixed trajectory cases to check for regressions in smoothness and impact geometry when upstream detectors or processing settings change.

subsections.title: Future directions
paragraphs: Future work would improve noise synthesis so training depends less on errors extracted from a particular detector. Extending synthetic data to coordinated human skeleton movement and refining virtual-camera sampling could also improve coverage of real motion and viewpoints.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: This project demonstrates independent research from an unavailable-data problem to a working sequence-reconstruction model, without upfront spending on new data collection or annotation. Synthetic motion made the research feasible; the resulting model produced smoother trajectories while preserving important impact behavior and extended to body-keypoint stabilization.
